variants.title: Bound a run
variants.context: Production LangChain wraps the orchestration graph in a contract: admit a run with identity, bind its budget, execute typed stages, then commit an outcome. Every accepted run needs bounded authority, a deadline, durable identity, and an observable outcome.
variants.prompt: A support application accepts a refund request that a graph will process. Put the contract steps in order, starting before any model call.

items.text: Execute typed stages, validating every state transition and tool argument while credentials and policy stay outside the prompt.
Authenticate the caller, authorize the use case, and assign run and thread identity with an idempotency key for the refund.
Set an absolute deadline, model and tool limits, a maximum loop count, a cancellation signal, and a spend envelope.
Commit a validated result, a truthful pending state, or a classified failure with release, trace, cost, and side-effect identifiers.

variants.hint: Ask what must already be true before the graph is allowed to execute anything.
variants.explanation: Identity and budget are decided before execution, and every run ends in a validated result, a truthful pending state, or a classified failure.

variants.title: Bound a run
variants.context: Production LangChain wraps the orchestration graph in a contract: admit a run with identity, bind its budget, execute typed stages, then commit an outcome. Every accepted run needs bounded authority, a deadline, durable identity, and an observable outcome.
variants.prompt: A worker restart resumes an existing thread. Put the contract steps in order for the resumed run.

items.text: Resume from the last checkpointed transition, revalidating state and tool arguments before any stage executes again.
Rebind the budget: keep the original absolute deadline and spend envelope, and attach a fresh cancellation signal.
Commit the outcome under the same run identity and record the trace, cost, and side-effect identifiers for diagnosis.
Authenticate the caller again and resolve the existing run and thread identity instead of minting a second business operation.

variants.hint: A resumed thread is the same business operation, not a new one.
variants.explanation: Resuming reuses the run identity and the original deadline, so a restart cannot silently become a second operation.

variants.title: Bound a run
variants.context: Production LangChain wraps the orchestration graph in a contract: admit a run with identity, bind its budget, execute typed stages, then commit an outcome. Every accepted run needs bounded authority, a deadline, durable identity, and an observable outcome.
variants.prompt: A tenant has already exhausted its spend envelope. Put the contract steps in order for the run that must stop early.

items.text: Skip stage execution, because no typed stage may run without an authority and a deadline behind it.
Bind the budget and discover that this tenant's spend envelope is already exhausted.
Authenticate the caller and assign run and thread identity so the rejected attempt stays traceable.
Commit a classified failure that names the exhausted budget rather than returning an empty success.

variants.hint: Even a run that never executes a stage still owes the caller an outcome.
variants.explanation: Budget binding happens before execution, and a refused run still ends in a classified, observable outcome.

variants.title: Reconcile before replay
variants.context: A timeout means the caller stopped waiting; it does not prove the dependency stopped working. The retry-safe path records intent in a checkpoint, sends one scoped attempt with a stable operation key, treats the system of record as the truth, and only then decides whether to return, replay, or escalate.
variants.prompt: A payment tool times out after it may have committed a refund. Put the retry-safe path in order.

items.text: The tool boundary sends one scoped request carrying that stable operation key and stores the dependency request ID.
The resume decision returns the existing result, replays only a proven non-commit, or escalates when the outcome cannot be established.
The system of record is queried by operation key, because it may have committed even though the response was lost.
The run checkpoint records the thread, step, operation key, deadline, and last confirmed transition.

variants.hint: Which participant actually knows whether the effect happened?
variants.explanation: Retry the smallest uncertain boundary, and reconcile with the authoritative service before replaying anything that can duplicate an effect.

variants.title: Reconcile before replay
variants.context: A timeout means the caller stopped waiting; it does not prove the dependency stopped working. The retry-safe path records intent in a checkpoint, sends one scoped attempt with a stable operation key, treats the system of record as the truth, and only then decides whether to return, replay, or escalate.
variants.prompt: A ticketing tool returns a connection reset while creating a customer ticket. Put the retry-safe path in order.

items.text: Look the operation key up in the ticket service, which exposes reconciliation for requests whose response was lost.
Send one scoped create-ticket request with that operation key and store the dependency request ID beside the checkpoint.
Return the ticket that reconciliation found, or replay only once the service proves that no ticket exists.
Checkpoint the thread, step, ticket operation key, and remaining deadline before the call leaves the graph.

variants.hint: A connection reset describes the caller's view, not the dependency's state.
variants.explanation: The operation key written before the attempt is what makes reconciliation possible afterwards.

variants.title: Reconcile before replay
variants.context: A timeout means the caller stopped waiting; it does not prove the dependency stopped working. The retry-safe path records intent in a checkpoint, sends one scoped attempt with a stable operation key, treats the system of record as the truth, and only then decides whether to return, replay, or escalate.
variants.prompt: A message tool succeeds, but the worker crashes before the graph records the result. Put the recovery in order.

items.text: It queries the messaging service by operation key and finds the message already delivered.
The resumed worker reads that checkpoint instead of replaying the graph from its first stage.
It records the confirmed side-effect ID and continues from the next transition rather than sending again.
The checkpoint still holds the intent, the operation key, and the deadline written before the send.

variants.hint: Replaying already successful stages costs money and can duplicate effects.
variants.explanation: Recovery starts from the checkpoint and the authoritative service, never from the top of the chain.

variants.title: Scope the state
variants.context: Memory is too broad to be a contract. Run context lives for one invocation, a checkpointer stores one thread's graph snapshots, a store holds cross-thread application memory, and the system of record owns business truth.
variants.prompt: A team is deciding where each piece of state belongs. Match each store to what it owns.

pairs.label: Run context
pairs.detail: Request-scoped identity, credentials, feature flags, deadline, and cancellation for one invocation.

pairs.label: Checkpointer
pairs.detail: Graph snapshots and pending writes for one thread, selected by a stable thread ID for resume and review.

pairs.label: Store
pairs.detail: Application-defined long-term information such as preferences, with tenant isolation, retention, and deletion rules.

pairs.label: System of record
pairs.detail: Payments, orders, and tickets, reconciled with the authoritative service instead of trusted from a snapshot.

variants.hint: Ask how long each item has to outlive the request.
variants.explanation: Separating state by lifetime and owner is what makes resume, deletion, and reconciliation possible.

variants.title: Scope the state
variants.context: Memory is too broad to be a contract. Run context lives for one invocation, a checkpointer stores one thread's graph snapshots, a store holds cross-thread application memory, and the system of record owns business truth.
variants.prompt: Match each store to the failure that appears when a team puts state in the wrong place.

pairs.label: Run context
pairs.detail: A secret is persisted into a prompt or a snapshot merely because a tool needed it during one invocation.

pairs.label: Checkpointer
pairs.detail: An unbounded message history grows until storage cost and context pressure slow every resume.

pairs.label: Store
pairs.detail: A preference written for one tenant is retrieved for another because isolation was never applied.

pairs.label: System of record
pairs.detail: A snapshot claims the refund completed while the payment service holds no such operation.

variants.hint: Each failure names the boundary that was crossed.
variants.explanation: Persist the minimum state needed to resume safely, and keep business truth in the authoritative service.

variants.title: Scope the state
variants.context: Memory is too broad to be a contract. Run context lives for one invocation, a checkpointer stores one thread's graph snapshots, a store holds cross-thread application memory, and the system of record owns business truth.
variants.prompt: Match each store to the question an operator answers by reading it.

pairs.label: Run context
pairs.detail: Which deadline and cancellation signal governed this single invocation?

pairs.label: Checkpointer
pairs.detail: Which recorded step should a resumed thread continue from?

pairs.label: Store
pairs.detail: Which long-term preferences may this tenant's later threads use?

variants.hint: One of these questions can only be answered outside your application.
variants.explanation: A checkpoint may record an operation ID, but only the authoritative service can confirm the business effect.

variants.title: Pick the control shape
variants.context: Choose the least autonomous architecture that completes the task. A deterministic pipeline suits a known path, an agent suits bounded tool choice, and a custom graph suits durable state with branches, approvals, and recovery.
variants.prompt: A nightly job reads each invoice, extracts the same seven fields, and writes them to a ledger. The order never changes. Which architecture is the strongest default?
options: A custom graph checkpointed after each invoice.
A deterministic pipeline of typed stages.
An agent that picks an extraction tool per invoice.
optionFeedback: Checkpoints buy recovery this job does not need, since a failed invoice can simply be rerun.
Right: the order and the allowed operations are known before execution, which makes typed stages easiest to test, budget, and explain.
An agent adds probabilistic routing to a path that is already fixed.
variants.hint: Ask what the model actually has to decide at run time.
variants.explanation: The strongest default is the smallest model of control that expresses the required decision.

variants.title: Pick the control shape
variants.context: Choose the least autonomous architecture that completes the task. A deterministic pipeline suits a known path, an agent suits bounded tool choice, and a custom graph suits durable state with branches, approvals, and recovery.
variants.prompt: A research assistant must consult an unknown number of read-only sources, choosing among four approved tools, before it can answer. Which architecture fits?
options: A fixed pipeline that calls all four tools on every request.
A bounded agent with explicit tool authority, an iteration limit, and stop conditions.
A durable graph that checkpoints after every lookup.
optionFeedback: Calling every tool wastes budget and still cannot decide when the evidence is sufficient.
Right: the model must select among approved tools and decide how many iterations are needed, inside explicit limits.
Durable checkpoints add operational weight that a short read-only run does not need.
variants.hint: Ask what the model actually has to decide at run time.
variants.explanation: Use an agent when tool choice and loop count are genuinely unknown, and keep authority, iterations, and stop conditions explicit.

variants.title: Pick the control shape
variants.context: Choose the least autonomous architecture that completes the task. A deterministic pipeline suits a known path, an agent suits bounded tool choice, and a custom graph suits durable state with branches, approvals, and recovery.
variants.prompt: A vendor onboarding process waits up to two days for an external compliance webhook and must continue from the last recorded step after a deployment restart. Which architecture fits?
options: One long agent call held open inside the API request handler.
A deterministic pipeline rerun from the start after each restart.
A custom graph with checkpointed state and an approval pause.
optionFeedback: A request handler cannot hold a two-day wait, and the run dies with the process.
Replaying the whole process after a restart repeats work and can duplicate external effects.
Right: explicit branches, checkpoints, and resumption at a known boundary are what a durable graph provides.
variants.hint: Ask what the model actually has to decide at run time.
variants.explanation: Durable state, approval pauses, and resumption at a known boundary are the requirements that justify a custom graph.

variants.title: Prove the release
variants.context: A successful HTTP response is not evidence that an LLM application worked. Production LangChain traces every causal boundary, evaluates behavior by slice, and proves that a rollback can handle state the new revision wrote.
variants.prompt: A service reports 99.9 percent HTTP success, but support tickets say the answers are wrong. What is the strongest next step?
options: Report the average score from the last offline evaluation run.
Raise the alerting threshold on terminal failure rate.
Sample production traces and score quality by task, cohort, and failure mode.
optionFeedback: One average across all cases is what let the regression through in the first place.
Failure rate is already healthy, which is exactly why it cannot explain wrong answers.
Right: service health and answer quality are separate signals, and one average hides the failing slices.
variants.hint: Ask which part of the system the current evidence actually touched.
variants.explanation: Trace the execution path and evaluate the product contract separately, then break results down by slice.

variants.title: Prove the release
variants.context: A successful HTTP response is not evidence that an LLM application worked. Production LangChain traces every causal boundary, evaluates behavior by slice, and proves that a rollback can handle state the new revision wrote.
variants.prompt: A release changes the checkpoint schema for a graph that has threads in flight. What must the team prove before deploying?
options: That the previous revision can read or deliberately reject state the new one writes.
That the new revision starts up faster than the current one.
That offline evaluation scores improved on the curated dataset.
optionFeedback: Right: a rollback is only real when the older revision can handle state written by the newer one.
Startup time says nothing about whether in-flight threads survive a rollback.
Quality gains do not make a rollback possible.
variants.hint: Ask which part of the system the current evidence actually touched.
variants.explanation: Checkpoint migration is a release gate: prove the rollback path before the new schema reaches production.

variants.title: Prove the release
variants.context: A successful HTTP response is not evidence that an LLM application worked. Production LangChain traces every causal boundary, evaluates behavior by slice, and proves that a rollback can handle state the new revision wrote.
variants.prompt: A load test drives the API handler to target throughput and passes cleanly. What did it fail to cover?
options: Request parsing and response serialization in the HTTP framework.
The replica count needed to accept inbound connections.
Queue wait, model quotas, checkpoint storage, and downstream concurrency.
optionFeedback: Parsing cost is already exercised by any request-level load test.
Connection capacity is precisely what the handler test measured.
Right: admission is only the entry point, and queued execution has its own limits that fail first under real load.
variants.hint: Ask which part of the system the current evidence actually touched.
variants.explanation: Load-test execution, not only admission, because API servers and queue workers scale on different signals.
